report.headline: Usage rate projected to fall to 17.8% from a G League 22.6%, but the true-shooting projection ties a trivial baseline and carries no signal

projection.text: The model projects a usage rate of 17.8% in the NBA, down from 22.6% in the source G League season, with an 80% interval of 12.5%–23.0% and a 95% interval of 9.8%–25.8%, against a target-league mean of 20.0% and standard deviation of 5.2%.

risks.text: The estimate rests on only 45 historical G League to NBA transitions, a thin cohort for a move this specific.
The 95% usage interval runs from 9.8% to 25.8%, nearly the full width of meaningful NBA roles, given a league standard deviation of only 5.2%.
The true shooting projection of 53.5% is not more accurate than simply guessing the league average, since its error (4.7%) equals the trivial baseline's error over the same 367 transitions.
Source-season assist rate was a modest 7.8% with a 9.2% turnover rate, suggesting a limited playmaking profile that could compress further in a reduced-usage NBA role.

strengths.text: Produced 20.062 points and 9.922 rebounds per 75 possessions in the source G League season.
Posted a true shooting percentage of 58.7% in the source season, 0.52 standard deviations above the G League average.
Carried a usage rate of 22.6% in the source season, 0.54 standard deviations above the G League average, indicating a featured offensive role.
The usage rate projection outperforms the best trivial baseline (3.3% mean absolute error versus 4.3%), so the drop to 17.8% projected usage is a metric worth trusting directionally.

uncertainty.text: The 80% usage interval alone spans 10.5 points, roughly two standard deviations of the target league's usage distribution, so the model can say this is a lower-usage profile than the source season but cannot pin down a specific number; the true-shooting projection of 53.5% should be read with no confidence at all, since its 4.7% mean absolute error exactly matches the trivial league-mean baseline over 367 held-out transitions.
